introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les deux questions de la Section Three.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (cohérence et organisation, présentation claire de la problématique, thèse, antithèse, synthèse et conclusion) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) sans barème chiffré par partie ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question (Q5 : 5 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 25 ; Q6 : 5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25) : aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), code 0790, JUNE 2023, trois heures.

Q1 : l'apeiron, la séparation des contraires, la sphère de flamme « comme l'écorce autour d'un arbre », la Terre libre au centre par équidistance, les roues de feu, l'origine marine du vivant et l'unique fragment sur la justice cosmique sont rapportés d'après Aristote, Théophrastus et la tradition doxographique, en paraphrase, sans citation littérale, sans date ni numéro de page. Le caractère matériel ou non de l'apeiron et la pluralité des mondes (successifs ou simultanés) sont discutés par les spécialistes ; le corrigé le dit sans trancher. Le sujet imprime « Anaximander's » : recopié tel quel.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (problematic).** Anaximander of Miletus (sixth century BC), traditionally presented as a pupil and successor of Thales, is one of the first thinkers to give a rational account of how the world came to be and why it is ordered as it is. A *cosmogony* is an account of the origin and formation of the cosmos. Almost nothing of his writing survives, so what we know comes mainly from later reports (Aristotle, Theophrastus and the doxographers). The problem is whether his cosmogony deserves to be called a success of early philosophy: does it truly explain the origin of the world by reason, or is it speculation still half dressed in myth?

**Thesis: the cosmogony is a bold and rational achievement.**
- *The first principle is the apeiron.* Thales had named water as the origin of all things. Anaximander asked how water could give rise to its own opposite, fire, and concluded that the source cannot be one of the determinate things that come from it. He called the source the *apeiron*, the boundless or indefinite: without limit in extent and without definite qualities, eternal and ageless, "encompassing" all things. Because it is indeterminate it can give rise to every definite thing.
- *Separation of opposites.* From the apeiron, through an eternal motion, the opposites (hot and cold, wet and dry) are "separated off". A sphere of flame forms around the air and mist surrounding the earth, as bark surrounds a tree. The world is thus produced by natural processes, without the action of gods.
- *Cosmic law.* The one fragment generally attributed to him says that things pay penalty and reparation to one another for their injustice according to the order of time. The balance of the opposites is imagined as a kind of justice: no element may dominate for ever. The cosmos is governed by an impersonal law.
- *Rational astronomy.* The earth is a free-floating body at the centre of the cosmos and stays in place because it is equally distant from everything, so there is no reason for it to move in one direction rather than another. This is an early use of the principle of sufficient reason. The heavenly bodies are rings or wheels of fire enclosed in mist, seen through openings.
- *Origin of life.* Living beings first arose in the moist element and were later modified; man is said to descend from fish-like creatures. This anticipates, in outline, later ideas of the evolution of life.

**Antithesis: the cosmogony has serious limits.**
- *The apeiron is hard to define.* An indefinite and unobservable principle cannot be tested by experience. It explains everything in general and nothing in particular: how the opposites separate out is not made clear, and the "eternal motion" is simply assumed.
- *Residual myth.* The language of injustice, penalty and reparation is moral and legal, borrowed from human society. The reasoning is rational in intention, but not yet scientific in method: there is no observation, measurement or experiment.
- *Errors of detail.* The cylinder-shaped earth, the wheels of fire and the account of the origin of man are wrong by later knowledge, and the plurality of worlds attributed to him (whether successive or coexisting) is uncertain.
- *Weak evidence.* Our knowledge depends on reports written long after him and read through Aristotle's categories, so his real position is partly reconstructed.

**Synthesis.** The weaknesses concern the content of his answers; the strength lies in the kind of question and answer he introduced. Anaximander replaced the myth of a divine birth of the world with a natural, law-governed process; he saw that a first principle must differ from the things it explains; and he used an argument from reason (the position of the earth) instead of authority. Judged by the standards of his time, the cosmogony is not complete or correct, but it is philosophically fertile: it opened the way for Anaximenes, Heraclitus, Parmenides and the atomists.

**Conclusion.** Anaximander's cosmogony is best assessed as a pioneering rational hypothesis rather than a finished theory. Its value is methodological: the idea of an indeterminate source, of a cosmos ordered by impersonal balance, and of explanation by reasoning alone mark the birth of Western philosophy and science. Its defects (untestable principle, borrowed moral imagery, factual errors) show how much remained to be done, but they do not remove its historical and philosophical importance.
